The AI Office is the Commission's function of contributing to the implementation, monitoring, and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, and AI governance [1]. It assists in the assessment of available standards [2] and may invite providers of general-purpose AI models and relevant national competent authorities to participate in the drawing-up of codes of practice [4]. The Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [3]. Member States shall facilitate the tasks entrusted to the AI Office [2]. The AI Office shall be allocated adequate resources to effectively perform its duties and exercise its powers in relation to the enforcement of this Regulation [3].

A provider who concludes that an AI system is not high-risk shall document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [1]. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2) [1]. Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider shall provide the documentation of the assessment [1].

The provider shall ensure that all necessary action is taken to bring the AI system into compliance with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation [3]. Where the provider of an AI system concerned does not bring the AI system into compliance with those requirements and obligations within the period referred to in paragraph 2 of this Article, the provider shall be subject to fines in accordance with Article 99 [3].

The provider shall ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market [5]. Where the market surveillance authority considers that the use of the AI system concerned is not restricted to its national territory, it shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay of the results of the evaluation and of the actions which it has required the provider to take [3].

The use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes shall comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions in relation to the use in accordance with the national law authorising the use thereof, in particular as regards the temporal, geographic and personal limitations. The use of the 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces shall be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment as provided for in Article 27 and has registered the system in the EU database according to Article 49. However, in duly justified cases of urgency, the use of such systems may be commenced without the registration in the EU database, provided that such registration is completed without undue delay. The use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes shall be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority in accordance with the national rules referred to in paragraph 5. The notification shall, as a minimum, contain the information specified under paragraph 6 and shall not include sensitive operational data.

An AI system is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or if the product whose safety component is the AI system is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that legislation. This classification applies regardless of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the product. [1]

An AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk under the following conditions:
1. It does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons.
2. It does not materially influence the outcome of decision making.
3. It is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review.
4. It is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III.
5. It is intended to perform profiling of natural persons.

The text mentions that AI systems intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns are not considered high-risk if they are not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review [3]. It also states that AI systems performing profiling of natural persons shall always be considered high-risk [1]. Therefore, the text does not provide a clear classification for tools specifically designed to detect cheating during exams. The AI Act passages provided do not answer this question.

A provider must report a serious incident immediately after establishing a causal link or becoming aware of it, and not later than 15 days under Article 73(1) or 10 days under Article 73(4) if the incident involves a high-risk AI system. The reporting period must account for the severity of the incident, and the notification must be made within seven days from the date the market surveillance authority receives the notification under Article 73(8).

The reporting deadline for a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system leading to someone's death is 10 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident, as stipulated in Article 73, paragraph 1. This period is subject to the severity of the incident and does not extend beyond the 10-day limit.

The AI Act does not explicitly mandate that a chatbot must explicitly state that it is talking to an AI system. However, Article 50 requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation applies to AI systems that are not authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Therefore, a chatbot must inform users that it is interacting with an AI system, provided the information is not obvious from the context of use.

[1] Article 50 states that deployers of an AI system generating or manipulating image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, or where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, in which case the disclosure is limited to the existence of such content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. [2] Article 3 defines a 'deep fake' as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful. The obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models include drawing up and keeping up-to-date technical documentation, including training and testing processes and evaluation results, which must contain the information set out in Annex XI for the purpose of providing it to the AI Office and national competent authorities [2]; drawing up and making publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training, according to a template provided by the AI Office [5]; drawing up and keeping up-to-date information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the general-purpose AI model into their AI systems [1]; putting in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [4]; and cooperating as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers pursuant to this Regulation [3].

According to Article 51(2), a general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. This threshold applies regardless of the number of registered end-users. [2]

Yes, general-purpose AI providers must comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, including the reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. This obligation is detailed in Article 53(c) of the Act.

The maximum fines for SMEs are determined by the lower of three specific percentages or amounts: the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99. In contrast, the maximum fines for SMCs are limited to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 4 and 5 of Article 99. Consequently, the maximum fines for SMEs are generally higher than those for SMCs, as the SMC limit is restricted to the lower of the two specified amounts, whereas the SME limit is the lower of the three specified amounts.

The difference between a provider and a deployer is defined in Article 3 of the Regulation. A provider is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that uses an AI system under its authority, whereas a deployer is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity [1].

The maximum administrative fine for a prohibited AI practice is EUR 35 000 000, which applies to non-compliance with Article 5. In contrast, the maximum administrative fine for breaching a deployer's obligations is EUR 750 000, which applies to non-compliance with Article 3. Therefore, the maximum fine for a prohibited practice is significantly higher than that for a breach of deployer obligations.

The EU AI Act does not recommend a specific AI chatbot for citizens; instead, it establishes a framework for AI safety and transparency. Citizens are encouraged to use AI tools that comply with the Act's requirements, such as the EU database for high-risk AI systems [4] and the provisions on prohibited AI practices [1]. The Act does not define a single "recommended" chatbot but mandates that all AI systems used must meet safety standards and transparency obligations [1][4].
